claims.text: An active-learning machine-learning surrogate trained on a limited subset of near-transition AIMD data can replace full AIMD in free-energy evaluations.
The surrogate can maintain phase free energies within approximately 5% of full AIMD results.
The proposed method can reduce computational cost by roughly a factor of ten relative to explicit AIMD.
The proposed method can outperform TOR-TILD for elemental and binary systems.
Elemental Fe and binary Fe-Ni near melting are representative target systems for the method.
Active learning can identify high-uncertainty configurations and use additional AIMD data to refine the surrogate.
The surrogate can capture electron-vibration coupling, anharmonicity, and vibrational entropy relevant to fusion thermodynamics.
Sampling from 0.8 to 1.2 times the estimated melting temperature is sufficient to cover the relevant near-transition regime.
Supercells containing 50–100 atoms are sufficient for the proposed solid- and liquid-phase calculations.
Sampling both NVT and NPT ensembles captures the thermodynamic fluctuations relevant to the proposed calculation.
Local atomic environments can represent anharmonic solid behavior, incipient disorder, developing liquid structure, and electron-vibration interactions.
Training preferentially on critical near-transition configurations allows the surrogate to mimic the ab initio energy landscape.
Mimicking the ab initio energy landscape enables the surrogate to reproduce the associated entropy contributions.
Using the surrogate within thermodynamic integration can replace many expensive AIMD runs while retaining comparable phase free energies and derived observables.
The approach should improve throughput especially for multicomponent systems in which TOR-TILD slows dramatically.
The method is valid for elemental and binary metallic systems around 0.8–1.2 times the melting temperature.

contradictions.description: The stated validity boundary is limited to elemental and binary systems, but the predicted benefit is emphasized for multicomponent systems. The hypothesis also claims superiority to TOR-TILD specifically for elemental and binary systems, leaving the principal multicomponent-throughput claim outside the defined test domain.
